text: Chapter 1 named Post-Incident Activity as the fourth NIST phase and called it a lessons-learned review. In a real SOC, that review is a scheduled meeting with a defined attendee list and agenda, held while the incident is still fresh — not a line in a closing ticket comment, and not something that only happens if there's time. An incident that's been contained and recovered from feels finished, but it isn't — this meeting is what actually makes the team better prepared for the next one.

A useful meeting pulls in everyone who touched the incident — analysts, the engineers who executed containment, the affected system owner, and often someone from management who can approve fixes. The agenda boils down to three questions asked about every phase of the response. What worked — the on-call page went out immediately, the EDR tool isolated the host cleanly. What didn't — a critical log source wasn't actually feeding the SIEM, or nobody knew who had authority to take a server offline. What should change — and every answer to that becomes a candidate action item.

NIST recommends holding this meeting soon after resolution — within days, not weeks — while the timeline and the friction the team hit are still fresh. Wait too long and the details blur: nobody remembers exactly why containment took 45 minutes instead of 15. For a major incident it stands on its own; smaller incidents can reasonably be batched into one periodic review.

Take a real example: a business email compromise, where a phished credential let an attacker set up a mailbox forwarding rule. What worked — the alert on that new rule fired within minutes and the analyst escalated correctly. What didn't — the team lost over an hour confirming MFA status, because nobody on the call had direct access to check it.

That one finding, captured only because the meeting happened, becomes a concrete fix: the on-call analyst now gets direct read access to MFA status, so that specific delay can't repeat. Skipping this meeting is how a SOC keeps relearning the same mistakes live. Next up: turning findings like this into a real after-action report.
